P1.evidence: The best setter-notes handling in the batch: 'I already got a lot of information from Kim, but I just want to do it the old-fashioned way, actually get to know you, get to hear it from you yourself, actually make sure that everything is [as] he told me.' He drew on those notes three separate times during the call. The frame carried two of four parts — 'we'll go over where you're at at the moment, where you want to go, see if we can help you actually bridge that gap' — with agreement sought and given ('How does that sound?' / 'Yeah, it sounds good'). The open question was never asked; the prospect invited it ('Go ahead and shoot away or ask away') and then narrated his own history. Four minutes of unstructured conversation about Bulgaria, gold panning and wartime Netherlands preceded the frame.

P2.evidence: The most consequential phase failure in this batch. Age, height and occupation all arrived because the prospect volunteered them; none was asked. Weight was never established at all. The health-conditions check was never put — and this is a man on haemodialysis with an indwelling catheter for stage five kidney failure. He volunteered the whole picture unprompted, which under the volunteered-information rule scores as a miss even though the rep then engaged with it substantively, asking about the dialysis schedule and the disequilibrium. What no version of engagement produced was a history: no medications, no blood pressure, no fistula or catheter site, no exercise restrictions, and above all no question about whether his nephrologist had cleared any of this. Injuries and movement limitations were never asked. Diet was never asked at any point, which matters clinically as well as commercially — a nutrition protocol was presented to a dialysis patient with no knowledge of what he eats, and the prospect himself had to raise potassium restriction. Sleep was never asked. The two hits are real: current training was asked directly ('are you doing any sort of workout at the moment?'), and energy was covered thoroughly through the good-days-versus-dialysis-days discussion. Results from current training drops out as not applicable because he does nothing.

P3.evidence: The bridge ran cleanly and early — 'And why now? Like, why do you think I need to do something?' — and produced the core material. The future-self question ran twice, once forward-looking ('how would that be when you're 65?') and once reframed after the prospect kept returning to negatives ('let's just look at the positive side for once'). The drive-through reached genuine depth, though almost all of it was prospect-supplied: the grandchildren of seven and four, the refusal to be the grandfather in a wheelchair with oxygen, and the single most powerful line in the corpus — 'I look at my dad and I'm looking into a window of the future. And I'm like, I don't want to be like this.' The rep did not ask for the aesthetics one-thing, did not ask what he cannot currently do, and did not ask who else this impacts; the grandchildren came up unprompted and were reflected back afterwards. The reflect-back was a personality summary rather than a reframe — 'you're mentally still 30 in your mind, right? You also always want to stay young, like Peter Pan.'

P4.evidence: Strong, though the prospect did much of the work himself. The full attempt history came out — collegiate wrestling, weightlifting, yoga, mountain biking, P90X, CrossFit, keto — and what happened with each was traced to a single repeating mechanism the prospect named precisely: 'about three or four months into it, there's a life something, whatever it might be, something triggers me. And then I fall off the rails.' He gave the specific instances too, the broken fingertip and COVID. The rep pressed the pattern rather than letting it pass — 'this is a transformation, this is not something we do for six months and then you just fall off' — and later tested it: 'Are you ready to commit to yourself to do that, but also to stick to it instead of falling off?' The gap was named by the prospect in the cleanest terms anywhere in this batch: 'I need somebody there to go, all right, Craig, let's get busy.' P4d is partial because the root-cause question was never actually asked, and P4f a miss.

P5.evidence: The settle question ran properly — 'it sounds like you're absolutely not willing to settle for a life where it's not going to get better. Is that true?' — and the line in the sand ran as a genuine question: 'Are you ready to commit to yourself to do that, but also to stick to it instead of falling off of the frame?' The two-year cost-of-inaction question was never actually put; the rep referenced having asked it ('we've just been talking about like the negative outcomes' and 'when I asked the question, it turns to not a good outcome') but the negative future was entirely prospect-generated. Why-not was never asked. Worth noting for coaching: with this prospect the consequence frame needed no construction at all — he arrived carrying it — and the rep correctly spent his effort pulling him toward the positive instead, which is a defensible read of the room even though it scores as unrun checks.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran in full form and drew an unambiguous answer: 'do you feel like if we have the nutrition, the workouts, and that one-on-one with Trevor locked in... that I'm actually going to be able to get to look better, feel better, and just get the energy to also play around with your kids and grandkids?' — 'there's no doubt that a transformation will begin. Yeah, I'm all down.' P6b was never asked, and here it would have been redundant in one direction and vital in the other: the prospect had already declared total willingness ('you don't have to convince me... I want to do it'), but the everything-you-needed question is also where a clinical or financial blocker would be forced into the open. P6c scores partial because the yes was genuine but came after the three pillars rather than before, and because the disqualifying fact — $400 to his name, disclosed at 00:36:47 — was already known and did not stop the presentation.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted, with the price presented at 00:48:00 and a six-instalment plan quoted, and no payment was collected. The rep then withdrew from the close on affordability grounds — 'because I really want to help you, of course, make that change, financially, of course, it's just not possible right now' — and set two calendar checkpoints instead. Nothing downstream of payment was reachable. Recorded here because the phase scoring cannot capture it: the rep did not discount, did not improvise a cheaper tier, and did not press a man with $400 to his name into a commitment, and that restraint is the strongest thing he did on this call.

objection_plays.detail: Unusually, the money conversation ran before the presentation rather than after, because the prospect raised it himself: 'Tell me what's involved... nothing's for free.' The rep asked directly — 'what are your finances looking like at the moment? Do you have anything available for yourself?' — and got the two decisive numbers, $400 liquid and about $2,000 a month fixed. Of the six financial-picture moves, cash on hand ran, income ran (though never surplus after expenses and medical bills), investments ran but only because the setter's notes had flagged an expected crypto withdrawal, and credit was raised and immediately dropped: 'I don't know if you have what your credit limit is' met 'I'm rebuilding my credit' and was not pursued. Isolation never ran, and the should-I-versus-how frame never ran. The judgement problem is not the play, it is the sequencing: having heard '$400 to my name' at 00:36:47, the rep presented $6,000 at 00:48:00 anyway, and the only plan he offered was the most expensive one.

Two clear timing triggers — money already committed to another practitioner this month, and a Florida trip being budgeted for September — and no OD move ran. The rep asked when the crypto position would resolve and converted the call into two scheduled check-ins. Given the prospect's actual position this is the humane and probably correct outcome, but it is a miss on the play rather than a run of it.

The clinical gap already logged in playbook.json, in its most acute form yet. Here the prospect never raised his condition as an objection — he raised it as motivation — so nothing in the process forced the question, and nothing in the script requires it to be asked. A man in active haemodialysis with an indwelling catheter, post-treatment cognitive impairment and stage five renal failure went through an entire sales process without one question about clinician clearance, and at the end was advised to buy a 12-16 kg kettlebell and start from a video. This is a structural failure of the script, not of the rep's warmth or intent, and it is the single strongest argument in this batch for a mandatory clinical gate in Phase 2.

Second gap: a competing health provider making a curative claim. The prospect disclosed that he had already committed $2,000 to an Ayurvedic practitioner who says she can heal his kidneys without dialysis or transplant, and that he disputes his own diagnosis. That is simultaneously a competing spend, a competing authority and a safeguarding concern, and there is no scripted move for any of the three. The rep probed once ('It doesn't sound like you 100% believe it') and then agreed with him: 'You can never 100% trust it.' Whatever the script should say here, it should not be that.

Third gap: funding a purchase from an unrealised speculative asset. The setter's notes flagged incoming crypto money, the closer raised it, and the entire follow-up plan is built on it — two calendar checkpoints keyed to whether a withdrawal completes. There is no rule about whether a prospect on disability income may be pipelined against an expected windfall, and no rule about what setters should and should not pass forward about a prospect's finances.

notes: Two judgements that have to be kept apart. On process, Phase 4 was strong and the rep held the price and walked away from a close he could not fund, which is the right commercial and human call and should be said plainly. On screening, this is the worst failure in the batch: Phase 2 ran two checks out of nine on a haemodialysis patient, diet was never asked before a nutrition protocol was prescribed, health conditions were never asked at all, and no clinician question was raised before advising him to buy a kettlebell and begin unsupervised. Coach the sequencing too — $400 to his name was known twelve minutes before $6,000 was presented, and the only instalment plan offered was the one this rep had told two other prospects that same week to avoid. The deeper items belong to the script and to the setter brief, not to this rep: there is no clinical gate anywhere in the process, and nothing tells a closer what to do when a prospect says he intends to stop dialysis.
